citations.quote: NetSat is a satellite formation composed of four 3U-CubeSats. It was launched on 28.9.2020 to demonstrate in orbit IoT approaches for realizing the interconnection functionality and the accessibility of all distributed ground and space system components.

The Compass middleware, which offers inherent IoT capabilities, was used to create a dynamic decentralized virtual mission network, which was active during all mission stages: satellite development, in-house and external satellite tests, and in-orbit operations. The middleware is an implementation of the Compass network protocol and standardized Compass services, and is used as a software and protocol basis for all NetSat satellite subsystems and all ground systems, which are involved in the mission: ground stations, mission control, formation control simulators and high precision test equipment.
We will show that this approach improved the realization process, the testability and controllability of space and ground systems in the NetSat mission.

This contribution is a summary of the main author's dissertation [7], which introduces ZfT's solution to the problem of monitor and control both ground and space segment systems as well as operation approaches that evolve from the IoT capabilities of the Compass protocol and services.

The space segment consists of four 3U CubeSats, whereat each satellite is composed of nine programmable subsystems: redundant on-board controller (OBC), redundant attitude and orbit control system (AOCS), five active panels, three electrical power systems (EPS), high-speed computing system and thruster control system.

One of the major tasks during the NetSat mission was to develop a common protocol stack, which allows all ground and space systems to communicate and cooperate with each other irrespective of their computational capabilities and communication link properties.

During the transition from single-satellite projects towards our first multi-satellite mission we had to find a way for small development teams to successfully achieve mission goals with continuously growing complexity in practically all areas.

The aim of the Model Tree Based Approach is to unify the way how software-driven functionality of a system is designed and offered. The functionality is represented by the system's Model Tree: functions, states, variables and other key-value entities. The model is accessed via the Model service. Most monitoring and controlling tasks are achieved by accessing and modifying the model values of the target system.

System's model does not only act as an interface for other systems instead it is also used by the system's software itself. All model values of a system are always in-sync with the actual software and hardware states. That is, the model approach is not only used to formalize the access to system capabilities it also acts as a software implementation pattern, which dictates how software components within a specific system communicate with each other by reading and writing corresponding local model values (model-based software design). Distributed cooperative tasks are achieved in a very similar manner with the only difference being that the corresponding components access and modify remote model values.

Following the MTBA approach the functionality of all systems is made uniformly accessible, hence introducing model-based communication. Every node can propagate on-demand its internal states, parameters, functions, sensor and control values as a hierarchically ordered model via the Model service. With Compass used as a carrier, all remote system models form a mission model (i.e. top-level digital twin), which represents the functionality, knowledge and current state of the entire mission.

Standard Compass services were implemented to enable commanding, model access and modification, file transmission, unit testing and dynamic code execution on remote systems. The protocol design was inspired by several existing protocols and standards, such as CCSDS PUS and MO services, CCSDS File Delivery Protocol and MQTT [10][11].

Compass protocol core and services were implemented for ultra-low power satellite subsystems (Compass OS) and for higher-level machines (CompassNode). Compass OS requires at least: 16 bit architecture, 2 kB RAM and 10 kB ROM thus allowing every existing satellite subsystem of the NetSat mission to enter the network as a discrete node. The Java-based CompassNode aims at more powerful systems in the ground segment (or NetSat computing module), it offers more advanced functions and is used as a middleware library in other software solutions, such as MATLAB, Orekit, Operations front-end, etc.

Due to the hardware abstraction layer, any software based on Compass OS becomes portable, i.e. the satellite software can be compiled and executed on workstations (with activated emulation for non-existent hardware components, such as flash memory).

With this functionality Model-driven development (MDE) became possible in the NetSat mission, i.e. many software components and cooperative processes were developed by following the Model $ \rightarrow $ Software $ \rightarrow $ Processor $ \rightarrow $ Hardware in-the-loop scheme [12].

The front-end was extensively used during all phases of the UWE-4 and NetSat missions by test engineers, simulation designers, satellite software developers, ground station advisers and satellite operators.

As soon as it is connected to the network it gains information about all currently available nodes from an incoming network beacon: addresses, network shape and characteristics of all hops (max. speed, max. packet size). The operator can select a node, access its model or perform any other supported action. In the meantime the front-end gradually learns about the capabilities of all previously operated nodes and caches the knowledge for later use.
Mission servers additionally store the entire Compass traffic, thus allowing the operators to reconstruct the entire mission model knowledge at any given time in the past.

During the tests the satellites were connected with serial cables to Compass front-end instances. With Compass the test execution and outcome was dramatically enriched as compared to the pre-Compass era.

Eventually the recording could either be re-played or the auto post-process was used to generate a traffic report: summary, log file with all detected Log service entries and separate CSV files for every model element containing all value changes.

Due to organizational reasons (and the COVID-19 situation) not all experts were able to support the test procedure on site - but they were able to access remotely connected satellites and supervise all subsystems during the test.

The Operations front-end offers the ability to record any operator actions. Recorded jobs are executed as soon as the desired target node becomes accessible in the network e.g. during an overpass. All created jobs are additionally visualized in the Schedule-View, which also shows future and past satellite overpasses.

Scripts can be used to read and modify local or remote model values, execute commands locally or remotely and access local file system.

Tiny scripts are written in the Operations front-end and then transmitted as pre-compiled byte-code to the remote Tiny service. Uploaded scripts can both be executed once or in a loop, and can also be loaded automatically during the boot-up. The operator can also convert recorded operation jobs to Tiny scripts and upload them for later in-orbit execution, thus enabling the on-board computer to reproduce in-orbit any possible operator's action (being only limited by the maximum script size).

During the LEOP phase multiple scripts were designed to switch on and off multiple subsystems during several orbits and periodically create reports, such as results of the I2C bus scanning or power consumption of subsystems during specific time periods. The logs were then automatically downloaded by the auto-operator and were used to evaluate the overall system performance.

The ability to execute dynamic code on all satellite subsystems and the code's ability to perform virtually any possible local and remote model access and modification became an essential satellite operations technology at ZfT. It allowed our team to promptly resolve observed issues and to quickly design new experiments based on new observations.

In NetSat two cooperation levels were tested: within the satellite (subsystem cooperation) and between the satellites. All experiments were designed as Tiny scripts, which were running on several cooperating subsystems. Examples of successfully performed intra-satellite cooperation: test new attitude control algorithms (OBC AOCS, Panels), earth imaging (OBC, computing board and Panels), reaction wheels test (OBC, AOCS, Panels and EPS) and GPS tests (OBC and Panels). Most of the experiments were performed using the Tiny's distributed computation capabilities, i.e. a script running on the OBC was dynamically creating scripts on other cooperating subsystems. The actual experiments were achieved using the Model service (model-based communication), e.g. AOCS setting magnetorquer actuator values located on panels by accessing corresponding panel model values.

To date three CubeSat missions with a total of 6 satellites (almost 60 individually accessible nodes in space) were realized with Compass. Due to the modeldriven philosophy new operation concepts became possible: self-configuring Compass Operations frontend, straightforward creation of cooperative tasks and cooperation between entirely different systems.

Based on the now available distributed computing capabilities, different distributed formation control mechanisms will be evaluated. Since the Tiny interpreter is permanently active in low-power mode, continuous formation control with more frequent update rates can now be established.

Such missions will still benefit from the existing dynamic mission network (routing, DTN) and uniform access to all already existing Compass-enabled nodes. In future machine learning techniques can be used to automatically detect anomalies based on the model knowledge or even perform model-based FDIR activities.

Mentioned approaches, Compass stack, Compass OS, CompassNode and Compass Operations front-end were developed by Veaceslav Dombrovski - more details can be found in his dissertation "Software Framework to Support Operations of Nanosatellite Formations" [7].
The NetSat operations were started one day after the launch on 29 September 2020.

Besides the verification tests performed at ZfT, NetSat EM and flight models were also tested at external facilities: temperature regulated vacuum chamber tests, acceptance shaker test and propulsion system test.

Cached models represent the knowledge of the entire mission and can be considered a high-level digital twin. Models cached on intermediate nodes can satisfy model requests without forwarding the request towards the actual destination, hence reducing ground to space traffic.

In NetSat operation schedules were ordered manually, so that the execution was performed in the ascending order. In future our team will implement schedule optimization techniques to automatically decide the execution order.

Unfortunately on 27 October 2020 the contact to NetSat-1 was lost and could not be recovered yet. Since the software on all four satellites is identical and the remaining satellites were still accessible and performed well, most probable explanation is a hardware failure.

In NetSat our team has established a decentralized mission control system, i.e. the operations were performed with multiple distributed instances of the Compass front-end located at ZfT, University of Wurzburg and home-office. Every instance was configured individually depending on the specific operator's interests.
The model-caching technique is not only active in the front-end, instead it is enabled on all CompassNodebased instances, such as server and front-end instances, simulations, etc.
